item.title: Norse Atlantic Airways files for bankruptcy and cancels all future flights
item.description:
Norwegian airline tells customers not to come to airports after surging fuel costs caused by Iran war ruin finances

Norse Atlantic Airways has filed for bankruptcy and cancelled all future flights after surging fuel costs caused by the Iran war ruined its finances.

The Norwegian airline said it was entering insolvency and posted a message on its website telling customers not to come to airports – including passengers potentially stranded away from home. Its collapse came a day after it put flights on hold with a warning that its finances were critical.

item.description:

Kuwait has summoned Iran's ambassador and handed him a protest note over "continuing Iranian attacks", the Kuwaiti foreign ministry said on Friday.

Iran has denied being behind the attack, while Kuwait and Italy have both blamed Tehran.

item.title: US broadcaster airs ad highlighting military aid to Israel during Saturday Night Live
item.description:
US broadcaster airs ad highlighting military aid to Israel during Saturday Night Live

Submitted by MEE staff on Fri, 11/27/2026 - 11:20
'Every three seconds, our government sends $400 of taxpayer money to Israel to do this,' says advert, over backdrop of amputee child in Gaza
A screengrab from the advert (No More For Israel)
Off

A 30-second advert highlighting US taxpayer funding for Israel was broadcast across the United States on Wednesday night during a Thanksgiving special edition of the long-running sketch show Saturday Night Live.

The ad, from the Institute for Middle East Understanding Policy Project (Imeu), a pro-Palestinian advocacy group based in California, shows an American girl carrying out chores over the course of the year in order to make $400 to buy a new bicycle. 

The footage then cuts from the American on a pristine suburban street to a Palestinian girl amid the rubble of Gaza. The Palestinian girl has lost a leg to Israeli bombs and is on crutches.

“Every three seconds, our government sends $400 of taxpayer money to Israel to do this,” says the ad's American narrator, against the backdrop of the girl in Gaza.

The US currently officially gives Israel $3.8bn a year, in a 10-year memorandum of understanding that runs from 2019 to 2028, working out at just over $360 every three seconds. 

The package also includes $3.3bn in foreign military financing and $500m in cooperative missile defence programmes, meaning that the advert's figure is accurate.

At the end of the ad, the viewer is directed to a website called No More For Israel, which tells you that "the US government has sent Israel over $330bn in inflation-adjusted dollars since 1948. That’s $400 every three seconds non-stop for nearly 80 years."

"Right now, behind closed doors, the White House is negotiating a new long-term weapons giveaway to Israel that is estimated to send at least $19bn more of our tax dollars to Israel over the next five years: another $400 every three seconds," the site says. 

'Antisemitic Hamas propaganda'

Israeli newspapers, the country's foreign ministry and pro-Israel figures in the US have hit out at broadcaster NBC for airing the advert.

End Jew Hatred, a group linked to the Lawfare Project, called the advert "antisemitic Hamas propaganda" and circulated a petition demanding that NBC stop broadcasting it.

Sex, drugs, Israeli tech and Trump rivalries: Five explosive claims from Kushner-UAE book
Read More »

Jonathan Greenblatt, CEO of the Anti-Defamation League, wrote on X: "Broadcasting an ad that blatantly demonizes the Jewish state and makes false claims about the use of American taxpayer dollars during primetime on the eve of a family holiday isn’t just insensitive. It’s indefensible.

"Again and again, why do people in positions of authority fail to demonstrate basic decency, let alone respect, for the Jewish community? At a moment of escalating antisemitism, there is no rationale to justify fanning the flames with such a twisted narrative."

Greenblatt did not elaborate on what the "twisted narrative" of the advert was or offer any evidence for why its claims were "false".

Self-described "accidental activist" Samantha Ettus said that the advert "promotes the lie that Israel deliberately targets children", more than 22,000 of whom have been killed in Gaza by Israel. "It never mentions Hamas. It never mentions October 7, the hostages, or the rockets Israel is defending against," Ettus posted on X.

Israel’s foreign ministry said: “Don’t let anyone exploit your loved ones’ compassion this holiday season. Ask who’s funding this campaign, whose real goal is the destruction of Israel.”

“We are airing this ad because the American people deserve to know where their money is going,” Margaret DeReus, Imeu's executive director, told Semafor.

Viewing figures for Wednesday's broadcast have yet to be released, but last year's Thanksgiving special attracted approximately 2.7 million viewers.

item.title: Was Andy Burnham right to accept his award from the Muslim-baiting Spectator?
item.description:
Was Andy Burnham right to accept his award from the Muslim-baiting Spectator?

Submitted by Peter Oborne on Thu, 11/26/2026 - 15:53
These cross-bench jollification ceremonies might appear innocent at a glance - until you dig deeper into the magazine's coverage of Islam
Andy Burnham speaks after being confirmed as the Labour Party’s new leader and Britain’s next prime minister, during a conference in central London on 17 July 2026 (AFP)
Off

The International Court of Justice (ICJ) finally ruled last week that the Myanmar government carried out a genocide when its army slaughtered thousands of Rohingya Muslims in an orgy of planned killing and mass rape.

This is the second time that the ICJ has found that genocide was committed against a Muslim population. Twenty years ago, it reached that verdict in the wake of the systematic execution of more than 8,000 Bosnian Muslims in Srebrenica.

That could become three times if the ICJ ultimately resolves that Israel’s ongoing slaughter of Palestinians in Gaza - where more than 74,000 have been confirmed dead so far, almost all of them Muslim - amounts to a genocide. 

The world has become an intolerably dangerous place if you are Muslim.

French writer Renaud Camus once warned that Muslim immigration would wipe out white Europeans. “The great replacement is very simple,” he said in 2012. “You have one people, and in the space of a generation you have a different people.”

Meanwhile, China has held hundreds of thousands of Muslims in secretive detention camps in recent years, while the Muslim community in India has been denounced as a “virus” by the chief minister of Uttar Pradesh. 

This view that Islam is a danger to humanity is impossible to substantiate. When Muslims travel to other countries, they normally arrive as victims of oppression, war or civil conflict, not as aggressors. 

Yet across much of the globe, Muslims are portrayed as the enemy - and that includes in Britain.

Islamophobic tropes

Pick up a newspaper. Read a book on current affairs. Consult a think tank. Listen to a politician. Go down to the pub. You will hear the same story: Islam is on the march, hell-bent on destroying the West.

Muslims are presented as invaders, enemies of civilisation, parasites, unpatriotic - uncomfortably similar to the tropes deployed before the Srebrenica and Myanmar genocides. 

According to the British Muslim Trust, there were 78 verified attacks involving mosques over the 12 months to July 2026. In recent decades, several Muslims have been murdered simply for being Muslim, while others get abused, targeted or beaten up. They fear going out at night. 

This past April, a man was jailed for 13 years after raping a Sikh woman because he believed she was Muslim.

It is easy to understand why some openly racist politicians dash along to Spectator events - and equally easy to understand why others failed to show 

Yet the systematic demonisation of Muslims has become a central part of the narrative of the British political and media classes in the 21st century. As I set out in my book The Fate of Abraham, this rhetoric has strong historical roots. But it is now so much a part of normal discussion that almost nobody notices. 

At Westminster in particular, there is an adamantine reluctance to challenge the demonisation of a relatively small section of the British population. Politicians are rightly wide awake to the problem of antisemitism, a poisonous virus that has been deeply embedded in western Christian DNA for a millennium of British history. 

But the majority of British MPs and newspapers flatly refuse to acknowledge that Islamophobia has become a problem in contemporary Britain.

Wednesday night provided a powerful and very telling example. Politicians from the main political parties gathered in central London to celebrate the Spectator Parliamentarian of the Year awards.

The most senior politicians in Britain were singled out for awards, including Prime Minister Andy Burnham and Tory leader Kemi Badenoch. Former foreign secretary David Lammy and Michael Gove, the former Tory cabinet minister who now edits the Spectator, presented the awards.

On the face of things, this was an admirable cross-party event, when journalists and politicians resolved for an evening to overcome their differences and celebrate the fact that we British have the good fortune to live in a parliamentary democracy. (The revered Spectator political columnist Henry Fairlie once memorably recorded that he slept more soundly in his bed when Parliament was sitting).

Troubling message

But let’s pause a moment and reflect on how all this good cheer and cross-bench jollification looks and feels if you are a British Muslim. This past summer, the Centre for Media Monitoring produced a report on the Spectator’s coverage of Islam. 

It found that the magazine’s extensive (one might even say obsessive) output on Islam portrays Muslims as invaders who don’t belong in this country, don’t share British values, and threaten our public spaces. 

The report also documents how Spectator writers substantiate this thesis through misrepresentations, fabrications, vulgar abuse, and conspiracy theories. Some of the examples are horrifying.

Many observers would regard such coverage as Islamophobic. Not the Spectator, which refuses to frame Islamophobia in its accepted sense as an irrational fear, hatred or prejudice directed at Muslims for being Muslim. 

How mainstream media fuels the UK's Islamophobia crisis
Read More »

Instead, it turns the concept on its head, arguing that the term is a cynical attempt to exempt Muslims from criticism, and to import a blasphemy law through the back door.

The magazine ran the headline: “There’s not enough Islamophobia in the Conservative Party.” After an outcry the Spectator changed the headline.

But one only has to imagine the career-ending consequences - not just for the writer, but also the editor, and indeed the magazine itself - that would (rightly) follow if a Labour magazine asserted “there’s not enough antisemitism in Labour”. 

Lammy might be interested to learn that the magazine recently ran two articles calling for the rehabilitation of the racist 20th-century Tory politician Enoch Powell.

Defenders of the Spectator are entitled to point out that Britain is a free country, and any magazine or newspaper is permitted to propagate whatever views it likes, no matter how bigoted or divisive, so long as they stay within the law. 

But that is not the case with political parties. When senior politicians accept awards, they do not send out a message that they agree with the organisers’ beliefs and objectives, and it would be absurd to claim that they do. Yet they are signalling that they regard the Spectator’s commentary on Muslims as within the boundaries of acceptable discourse. 

It is easy to understand why some openly racist politicians dash along to Spectator events - and equally easy to understand why others, like Zack Polanski’s Green Party, failed to show. 

When Burnham accepted his well-deserved award as politician of the year (last year’s recipient was Reform UK leader Nigel Farage), he was not endorsing the Spectator’s compulsive hostility to Muslims. But he certainly was sending the message that the Spectator operates within the acceptable boundaries of public discourse when it demonises Muslims. 

That is a troubling message to send out at any time - all the more so as Islamophobia Awareness Month reaches its climax.

The views expressed in this article belong to the author and do not necessarily reflect the editorial policy of Middle East Eye.
